title: Switching: MAC table, collision and broadcast domains

videos.script: A switch looks like it does nothing. You plug in cables and everything talks. {{switch}} In fact it keeps a table, and every decision it makes comes from that table. It learns from the address a frame comes from, and uses it for the address the next frame goes to. {{table}} In the lab you will watch the table fill from a single ping, and see its timers count. {{learn}} Then you will send frames to an address that nobody has. The switch cannot learn it, so it sends those frames out of every port, and a third computer catches them. {{flood}} Two words come with switching, and both are about who hears what. A collision domain is who has to take turns. A broadcast domain is how far a question to everybody reaches. {{domains}} You will see an ARP question reach every computer on the switch, and stop dead at the router. {{router}} Last, you will lock a port so that only one address may use it. One computer is refused, then let in, then refused again when it changes its own address. {{lock}} That last step shows what a MAC address can prove, and what it cannot.
